headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Wound Dressing
headings.content: A wound dressing is a therapeutic material applied directly to a wound or injured body tissue to protect it from further harm and promote optimal healing. In clinical nursing practice, understanding wounds and their coverings is foundational for preventing healthcare-associated infections, managing exudate, and restoring skin integrity. A wound itself is defined as a disruption of the normal anatomical structure and function of the skin and underlying tissues, which can be caused by physical, chemical, thermal, or immunological insults. When nurses apply a dressing, they create a specialized microenvironment that supports cellular processes necessary for tissue repair, such as angiogenesis and epithelialization. The choice of dressing depends on various clinical parameters, including the depth of the tissue loss, the amount of wound drainage, the presence of infection, and the overall health status of the patient. Nigeria's tropical climate and specific health challenges, such as the high prevalence of chronic ulcers and traumatic injuries, demand that nursing students master both traditional and modern wound management concepts. By grasping the basic definition and scope of wound dressings, student nurses can bridge classroom theory with practical bedside care, ensuring that every patient receives individualized, evidence-based interventions tailored to their specific wound etiology.

headings.title: Purposes and Objectives of Wound Dressing
headings.content: The application of a wound dressing serves several vital physiological and clinical objectives aimed at accelerating recovery and preventing complications. First and foremost, a dressing acts as a physical barrier against external pathogenic microorganisms, significantly reducing the risk of local and systemic infections. Second, it helps maintain a moist wound environment, which contemporary scientific evidence proves is superior for cellular migration, collagen synthesis, and rapid epithelialization compared to dry healing. Third, dressings are designed to absorb excess exudate and toxic components, preventing the maceration of healthy periwound skin while managing fluid drainage effectively. Additionally, dressings provide mechanical protection from accidental trauma, offer thermal insulation to keep the wound bed at an optimal physiological temperature of around 37 degrees Celsius, and can help achieve hemostasis during the initial stages of injury. For nursing students in clinical settings, evaluating these objectives helps determine the appropriateness of a selected dressing material. Furthermore, dressings can immobilize the surrounding area to reduce tension on wound edges, control localized pain, and eliminate dead space within deep wounds where fluid could otherwise accumulate and form abscesses.

headings.title: Classification and Types of Wounds
headings.content: Wounds can be classified using several different criteria, including their etiology, depth of tissue involvement, and the cleanliness or contamination level of the wound bed. Based on etiology, wounds are broadly divided into acute wounds, such as surgical incisions, lacerations, and burns, which typically follow a predictable and timely healing trajectory, and chronic wounds, such as diabetic foot ulcers, venous leg ulcers, and pressure injuries, which stall in the inflammatory phase and fail to heal in an orderly timeframe. Regarding depth, partial-thickness wounds involve damage to the epidermis and partial dermis, whereas full-thickness wounds extend through the dermis into subcutaneous tissue, muscle, or bone. Furthermore, surgical and traumatic wounds are categorized by their degree of microbial contamination: clean wounds (uninfected with no inflammation), clean-contaminated wounds (involving the GI, respiratory, or genitourinary tracts under controlled conditions), contaminated wounds (open, fresh accidental wounds with major breaks in aseptic technique), and dirty or infected wounds (containing old traumatic wounds with retained devitalized tissue or clinical signs of infection). Understanding these classifications enables student nurses to anticipate healing complications, choose appropriate dressing categories, and communicate effectively with the multidisciplinary healthcare team.

headings.title: Types of Dressing Materials and Their Indications
headings.content: The market offers a wide variety of dressing materials, and nurses must match the correct product to the specific clinical presentation of the wound. Traditional dressings include woven gauze and non-woven sponges, which are inexpensive and commonly used for mechanical debridement, packing, or covering clean, dry surgical wounds, though they tend to adhere to the wound bed if allowed to dry out. Modern dressings are engineered to optimize the wound microenvironment and include films, hydrocolloids, foams, alginates, and hydrogels. Transparent film dressings are thin, polyurethane sheets coated with an adhesive; they are permeable to gas and moisture vapor but impermeable to liquids and bacteria, making them ideal for superficial wounds or IV sites with minimal exudate. Hydrocolloid dressings contain gel-forming agents in an adhesive compound laminated to a flexible backing, creating a moist environment that autolytically debrides necrotic tissue, making them suitable for low-to-moderate exudating chronic wounds. Foam dressings are polyurethane sponges that provide high absorbency and thermal insulation, perfect for moderate-to-heavy exudating wounds. Alginates, derived from seaweed, form a hydrophilic gel when they interact with wound exudate, making them exceptionally useful for bleeding or heavily draining wounds. Hydrogels supply moisture to dry, necrotic, or slough-laden wound beds to promote autolytic debridement. By understanding these indications, nursing students can make sound clinical judgments during patient care simulations and hospital rotations.

headings.title: Assessment of Wounds and Patient Preparation
headings.content: Before performing any wound dressing procedure, a comprehensive assessment of both the patient and the wound must be conducted to establish a baseline and guide therapeutic interventions. The nurse begins by reviewing the patient's medical history, nutritional status, underlying comorbidities like diabetes or vascular disease, and current medications, such as corticosteroids or anticoagulants, which can impair healing. Pain assessment is crucial, and the nurse should premedicate the patient if necessary before the dressing change. During the wound assessment, the nurse inspects the location, dimensions (length, width, and depth), shape, and tissue types present in the wound bed, such as granulation tissue (red/pink), slough (yellow/white), or eschar (black/necrotic). The nurse also evaluates the periwound skin for erythema, maceration, edema, or induration, and observes the character, color, consistency, and odor of any exudate. Patient preparation involves explaining the procedure clearly to gain informed consent and alleviate anxiety, ensuring privacy, positioning the patient comfortably, and gathering all necessary supplies at the bedside before opening sterile packages. This systematic approach ensures patient safety, minimizes discomfort, and promotes thorough clinical documentation.

headings.title: Aseptic Technique and Infection Control Principles
headings.content: Infection control principles and the strict application of aseptic technique are the absolute cornerstones of safe wound management. Aseptic technique encompasses practices aimed at minimizing contamination and protecting the patient from healthcare-associated infections during invasive or clean procedures like dressing changes. This involves strict hand hygiene before and after patient contact, the use of appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) such as gloves, aprons, and masks, and the careful establishment of a sterile field. When opening sterile supplies, nurses must maintain the integrity of the sterile barrier, ensuring that only sterile instruments or gloved hands touch sterile items, and that any item falling below waist level or touching a non-sterile surface is immediately discarded. Furthermore, cleaning principles require working from the cleanest area to the dirtiest area, which for a surgical incision means cleaning directly over the wound first and moving outward toward the periwound skin, whereas for an open, draining ulcer, it may involve cleaning from the center of the wound outward in a circular motion. Nursing students must rigorously practice these techniques to prevent introducing exogenous microorganisms into vulnerable tissues, thereby safeguarding patient recovery outcomes.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Performing a Wound Dressing
headings.content: Executing a wound dressing change requires a systematic, step-by-step approach to ensure clinical effectiveness and patient safety. The procedure begins with verifying the medical order, gathering all equipment (sterile dressings, cleansing solutions, waste bags, PPE, and measuring tools), and performing hand hygiene. The nurse introduces themselves, identifies the patient, explains the procedure, screens for privacy, and positions the patient so the wound is easily accessible while maintaining dignity. The nurse puts on clean, non-sterile gloves and carefully removes the old dressing, noting the type, amount, and odor of any drainage on the removed material. If a dressing sticks, it should be moistened with sterile normal saline to ease removal and prevent disrupting fragile new tissue. After removing the old dressing, the nurse discards it along with the gloves, performs hand hygiene, and sets up a sterile field. Putting on sterile gloves, the nurse cleans the wound bed using the appropriate antiseptic or normal saline solution according to the established cleaning principles. Once cleaned and dried gently with sterile gauze, the nurse applies any prescribed topical agents, places the appropriate primary and secondary dressings, and secures them securely with tape or bandages. Finally, the nurse disposes of all contaminated waste safely, helps the patient into a comfortable position, performs hand hygiene, and documents the procedure.

headings.title: Documentation and Evaluation of Wound Healing
headings.content: Accurate documentation and continuous evaluation are critical nursing responsibilities that ensure continuity of care and monitor the patient's healing progress. Documentation of a wound dressing change must be prompt, objective, and comprehensive, detailing the exact date and time, the location and appearance of the wound, the characteristics and volume of exudate, the condition of the periwound skin, the type of cleansing solution and dressing materials applied, the patient's tolerance of the procedure, and any education provided. Vague statements such as 'wound looks better' must be avoided in favor of measurable descriptions, such as 'sacral pressure ulcer measuring 4cm by 3cm with a depth of 0.5cm; moderate serosanguineous drainage noted; edges intact with mild erythema; covered with hydrocolloid dressing.' Evaluation involves comparing current wound assessments against baseline data recorded during initial evaluations. If a wound shows signs of delayed healing, increased pain, expanding redness, foul odor, or purulent discharge, the nurse must report these findings to the attending physician and collaborate on modifying the care plan. For nursing students, mastering this documentation ensures legal protection, effective interprofessional communication, and high standards of clinical accountability.

headings.title: Common Complications of Improper Wound Management
headings.content: Improper wound management can lead to a cascade of serious local and systemic complications that prolong hospital stays, increase healthcare costs, and threaten patient survival. One of the most common complications is wound infection, which occurs when bacteria proliferate in the wound bed, leading to clinical signs such as localized pain, swelling, warmth, purulent discharge, and systemic symptoms like fever and leukocytosis. Another major complication is wound dehiscence—the partial or complete separation of outer wound layers—and evisceration, where internal visceral organs protrude through the opened surgical wound, representing a severe surgical emergency requiring immediate sterile saline-soaked dressings and surgical intervention. Maceration of the periwound skin frequently results from using dressings with inadequate absorption capacity or failing to manage heavy exudate, leading to skin breakdown and a larger wound surface area. Conversely, desiccation occurs when a wound is allowed to dry out completely, delaying cellular migration. Other complications include fistula formation, sinus tracts, hypergranulation tissue, and the development of chronic, non-healing wounds. Student nurses must remain vigilant, recognizing early warning signs of these complications to intervene promptly and prevent devastating patient outcomes.
